title: Southern Italy's Treasury of Native Grapes
quiz.0.question: Nerello Mascalese is called "the Italian Pinot Noir" mainly because…?
quiz.0.options.0: Both are variants of Pinot Noir
quiz.0.options.1: Nerello Mascalese has a light, elegant style, fine tannins and a very strong expression of terroir
quiz.0.options.2: Both are mainly grown in the cold climate of northern Italy
quiz.0.options.3: Both are famous for sparkling wine
quiz.0.explanation: Although Nerello Mascalese grows on Mount Etna in Sicily (Italy's far south), its wines show a lightness and elegance like Burgundian Pinot Noir — pale ruby colour, fine tannins, high acidity and a very strong expression of terroir (volcanic minerality) — hence "the Italian Pinot Noir".
quiz.1.question: What does "Vulture" refer to in Aglianico del Vulture DOC?
quiz.1.options.1: Monte Vulture, an extinct volcano in Basilicata, on whose slopes Aglianico is grown
quiz.1.options.3: Latin for "strength", describing Aglianico's powerful structure
quiz.1.explanation: Vulture is Monte Vulture (1,327 m), an extinct volcano in Basilicata. Aglianico is grown on its slopes (300-700 m), and the volcanic soils give the wine its distinctive minerality and structure.
quiz.2.question: Gaglioppo is the signature grape of which region?
quiz.2.explanation: Gaglioppo is the signature grape of Calabria at the toe of Italy, mainly in Cirò DOC (Calabria's most important DOC). Cirò is considered one of Italy's oldest wines, with a history going back to Greek colonisation.
quiz.3.question: What does the name Negroamaro mean?
quiz.3.options.1: "Black bitter", known for its dark colour and noticeably bitter finish
quiz.3.explanation: The name Negroamaro is often explained as "Negro (black) + Amaro (bitter)", describing the grape's defining traits: deep black skins and a slightly bitter finish in the wine; another theory traces it to Latin niger and Greek mavros, both meaning "black".
quiz.4.question: What is the relationship between Primitivo and Zinfandel?
quiz.4.options.0: None at all; they just look similar
quiz.4.options.1: Zinfandel is a descendant of Primitivo
quiz.4.options.2: They are the same variety, originating in Croatia (Tribidrag/Crljenak), developed separately in Italy and the US
quiz.4.options.3: Primitivo is an improved version of Zinfandel
quiz.4.explanation: DNA comparison (UC Davis research, 1994) proved that Primitivo and Zinfandel are the same variety, and in 2001 it was traced further to Croatia's Crljenak Kaštelanski (old name Tribidrag). It reached southern Italy in the 18th century and the US in the 19th, developing different personalities in different terroirs.
quiz.5.question: For Nerello Mascalese in Etna DOC, which geographical factor is the most crucial element of terroir?
quiz.5.options.0: Warmth from the Mediterranean maritime climate
quiz.5.options.1: Etna's high elevation (500-1,000 m) and volcanic basalt soils
quiz.5.explanation: Etna DOC's core advantage is the volcano's high elevation (500-1,000 m), bringing a cool climate (large day-night temperature swings), a very long growing season and mineral-rich volcanic basalt soils — together these create Nerello Mascalese's lightness, elegance and deep minerality.
quiz.6.question: Among the South's native grapes, which is one of the most widely planted in Puglia, known for deep colour and easy drinking?
quiz.6.explanation: Negroamaro is one of Puglia's most widely planted grapes, centred on Salice Salentino DOC (the Salento peninsula), known for deep black colour, rich fruit and a bitter finish — both Puglia's "volume workhorse" and a "fine-wine flagship".
slides.0.title: Southern Italy's Treasury of Native Grapes
slides.0.subtitle: Nerello Mascalese · Aglianico · Gaglioppo · Negroamaro · Primitivo · Greco · Fiano — great grapes of volcano, sun and sea
slides.1.title: Nerello Mascalese — Etna's "Italian Pinot Noir"
slides.1.content:
Why "Italian Pinot Noir"?

Nerello Mascalese grows on the slopes of Mount Etna, Sicily's active volcano, and is Italy's most astonishing paradox — it grows in the hottest part of southern Italy, yet makes extremely light, delicate, high-acid reds whose style is closer to northern Italy or Burgundy than to the typical south. This contrast is the magic of Etna.

Area: Etna DOC (Sicily) | Elevation: 500-1,000 m | Soils: volcanic basalt | Climate: cool at altitude + volcanic minerality

Grape Profile

Appearance: pale ruby to medium depth (far paler than a typical southern red)
Aromas: fresh red berries (strawberry, raspberry), rose, violet, blood orange, volcanic minerality (volcanic rock, smoke, flint)
Palate: fine, delicate tannins, high acidity, medium body | not a "heavy southern style" at all, but "light Burgundian character"
Ageing: top wines age 10-20 years; old-vine versions (vines 60-100+ years old are fairly common on Etna) are even more complex
slides.2.title: Etna DOC — Italy's Hottest Rising Star
slides.2.content:
The Area's Structure: North vs South

Etna Rosso DOC (north slope): the north slope (around Castiglione di Sicilia and Randazzo) is generally seen as the best exposure, centred on places such as Solicchiata and Passopisciaro, with dense old vines and the greatest mineral complexity. Leading names: Cornelissen, Benanti, Terre Nere, Passopisciaro
East and south slopes: Milo on the east slope is the heart of Etna Bianco Superiore; the south slope gets more sun, giving slightly fuller wines with a little less minerality, suited to earlier drinking

Top Producer Profiles

Frank Cornelissen: a Belgian incomer and natural-wine pioneer. His flagship Magma (old vines, tiny yields) and the Munjebel range are made with almost no added sulphur and fermented in clay vessels — the summit of natural wine on Etna
Benanti: founder of Etna's modern fine wine (1988), whose Serra della Contessa (Viagrande, south-east slope), Rovittello (north slope) and Pietra Marina (Etna Bianco Superiore) established Etna's international reputation
Terre Nere (black earth): Marc de Grazia (a wine importer turned grower) was among the first to bottle single plots from individual contrade, championing Etna's contrada terroir concept

Etna's Rise

1968: Etna DOC was created, Sicily's first DOC, but long remained obscure
2000s: after Benanti, incoming producers such as Cornelissen, Terre Nere and Passopisciaro (Andrea Franchetti) drove a revival
From 2011: the Etna DOC rules officially recognise 133 contrade, which may appear on labels; strong praise from international critics has made Etna one of Italy's most watched areas
Opportunity: many old vines and low-profile growers are still undiscovered by the mainstream market, and new north-slope contrada wines are the next focus
slides.3.title: Aglianico — Southern Italy's Greatest Red Grape
slides.3.content:
"The Barolo of the South"

Aglianico is widely regarded as southern Italy's greatest red grape, known for its striking tannic structure, high acidity and very long ageing potential (20-30 years), and critics have dubbed it "the Barolo of the South". It has two core areas: Taurasi DOCG (Campania) and Aglianico del Vulture (Basilicata, DOC; the Superiore is DOCG). Each has its own style, forming one of the most interesting same-grape terroir comparisons in Italian wine.

Core areas: Taurasi DOCG (Campania) vs Aglianico del Vulture DOC / Superiore DOCG (Basilicata)

Taurasi vs Aglianico del Vulture in Depth

Taurasi DOCG (Campania): volcanic hills at 400-700 m, clay-limestone soils. Legal minimum ageing 3 years (Riserva 4 years). A weightier style with stronger tannins and black fruit + tar + leather complexity, with 20-30 years' ageing potential. Top names: Mastroberardino (Radici), Feudi di San Gregorio, Terredora di Paolo
Aglianico del Vulture DOC (Basilicata): the slopes of the extinct Monte Vulture volcano (300-700 m), volcanic tuff soils. The DOC is released after about 1 year; the Superiore DOCG needs at least 3 years' ageing, Superiore Riserva 5 years. A more elegant style with more pronounced minerality (volcanic character), red berries + a distinctive smoky volcanic-ash note, ageing 15-25 years
Shared grape traits: one of Italy's latest-picked grapes (late October to early November), high tannin, high acidity, low pH; very hard to approach when young, it needs a lot of time to show its complexity
slides.4.title: Gaglioppo & Negroamaro — Pride of Italy's Heel and Toe
slides.4.content:
Gaglioppo — Calabria's Ancient Greek Heritage

History: Cirò DOC is one of Italy's oldest wines; Greek colonists (Magna Graecia) planted vines on the Calabrian coast, and legend says it was the victory wine of Olympic athletes, with a history of over 2,700 years
Grape profile: deep ruby, blackberry + redcurrant + white pepper + Mediterranean herbs (rosemary, thyme), medium-high tannin, high acidity | ages 8-15 years
Top producers: Librandi (Duca Sanfelice Riserva), A. Caparra & C. Siciliani (traditional fermentation)

Negroamaro — The Black Soul of Salento, Puglia

Meaning of the name: often explained as Negro (black) + Amaro (bitter); another theory traces it to Latin niger and Greek mavros, both meaning "black" — the deep black skins and slightly bitter finish are the grape's defining traits and its "flavour fingerprint"
Main area: Salice Salentino DOC (the Salento peninsula, Puglia) | deep purple-black, black plum, dark chocolate, fennel, Mediterranean herbs + a bitter finish
Two styles: Rosso (full-bodied, 12-18 months in oak, ages 10-15 years) vs Rosato (famous as a deep-coloured rosé, one of Italy's best pinks) | Top names: Leone de Castris (Five Roses Rosato), Candido
slides.5.title: Primitivo, Greco and Fiano — The Many Faces of the South
slides.5.content:
Primitivo = Zinfandel

Puglia | Primitivo di Manduria DOC/DOCG

Shared DNA: UC Davis research in 1994 proved it is the same variety as Zinfandel (US); in 2001 it was traced to Croatia's Crljenak Kaštelanski, later confirmed under its old name Tribidrag
Style differences: Italian Primitivo is drier than Californian Zinfandel, with purer black fruit and tighter tannins; Californian Zin is jammier with higher alcohol (15-16%)
Dolce Naturale (sweet): made without added spirit or sweeteners, from the natural sugar of late-picked or lightly dried grapes, keeping noticeable residual sugar; a separate DOCG since 2011, it is Primitivo's fine sweet wine

Greco di Tufo DOCG

Campania | DOCG

The name Tufo: "tufo" is Italian for tuff (a volcanic deposit) and also the name of the area's core village; the local tuff and sulphur-bearing soils (Tufo once had sulphur mines) give Greco whites a distinctive salty minerality and smokiness
Flavours: white peach, apricot, citrus peel, stone + a characteristic sulphurous minerality (a "struck flint" note)
Top names: Feudi di San Gregorio (Cutizzi single vineyard), Mastroberardino (Novaserra)

Fiano di Avellino DOCG

Campania | DOCG

Origin of the name: one theory derives it from the Latin Vitis apiana ("the vine bees love"), as its sweet berries attract bees
Flavours: honey, pear, hazelnut, white flowers, white mushroom + a creamy finish | the elegant counterpart to Greco — Greco is more mineral and taut, Fiano rounder and creamier
Top names: Feudi di San Gregorio (Pietracalda), Ciro Picariello, Colli di Lapio (Clelia Romano)

The South's Two Great Whites Compared

Greco di Tufo: strongly mineral, taut acidity, sulphurous flint notes | with oysters, seafood
Fiano di Avellino: round and creamy, honey and hazelnut | with lobster risotto, soft-shell crab
In common: both have great ageing potential (8-15 years) and are among Italy's most underrated top whites
slides.6.title: The South's Five Great Grapes Compared
slides.6.content:
Nerello Mascalese

Red | Etna DOC (Sicily's volcano)

Light and elegant / volcanic minerality / the Italian Pinot Noir / ages 10-20 years / the fastest-rising international reputation in recent years

Aglianico

Red | Taurasi DOCG / Aglianico del Vulture DOC

The South's greatest / high tannin, high acid / ages 20-30 years / the Barolo of the South / picked late, end of October

Gaglioppo / Negroamaro

Red | Cirò DOC (Calabria) / Salice Salentino (Puglia)

Ancient Greek heritage / Mediterranean herbs / Negroamaro famous for Rosato / excellent value

Greco di Tufo / Fiano di Avellino

White | Campania's two DOCG greats

Greco: mineral and flinty / Fiano: round and honeyed / both age 8-15 years / Italy's most underrated top whites
slides.7.title: Key Takeaways
slides.7.points.0: Nerello Mascalese: Mount Etna (500-1,000 m), light and elegant, the Italian Pinot Noir; Frank Cornelissen, Benanti and Terre Nere are top producers; its international reputation has risen fast in recent years
slides.7.points.1: Etna DOC: the north slope outperforms the south; old-vine contrada wines have the greatest complexity; since 2011, 133 contrade may be named on labels
slides.7.points.2: Aglianico: the South's greatest red grape, "the Barolo of the South"; Taurasi DOCG (Campania) vs Aglianico del Vulture DOC (Basilicata) is the most exciting same-grape terroir comparison
slides.7.points.3: Gaglioppo / Cirò DOC: over 2,700 years of history going back to Greek colonisation; Mediterranean herbs + blackberry flavours
slides.7.points.4: Negroamaro: often explained as "black bitter"; one of Puglia's most important grapes; Leone de Castris's Five Roses Rosato is one of Italy's best rosés
slides.7.points.5: Primitivo = Zinfandel = Tribidrag (DNA: proved identical to Zinfandel in 1994, Croatian origin traced in 2001); Primitivo di Manduria Dolce Naturale DOCG is the benchmark fine sweet style
slides.7.points.6: Greco di Tufo DOCG: tuff soils → mineral, flinty character; Fiano di Avellino DOCG: round, honey and hazelnut; both can age 8-15 years
slides.7.points.7: Food: Nerello Mascalese with grilled tuna / Aglianico with Neapolitan slow-braised beef / Negroamaro Rosato with octopus salad / Fiano with lobster
slides.8.title: Southern Native Grapes Knowledge Check
slides.8.questions.0.question: Why is Nerello Mascalese called "the Italian Pinot Noir"?
slides.8.questions.0.options.0: It is a genetic descendant of Pinot Noir
slides.8.questions.0.options.1: Light elegance, fine tannins and a very strong expression of volcanic terroir
slides.8.questions.0.options.2: It is mainly grown in the cold climate of northern Italy
slides.8.questions.0.options.3: It is famous for sparkling wine
slides.8.questions.0.explanation: Although grown on a Sicilian volcano in the south, Nerello Mascalese shows the lightness and elegance of Burgundian Pinot Noir — pale ruby, fine tannins, high acidity and a very strong expression of volcanic terroir (minerality) — hence "the Italian Pinot Noir".
slides.8.questions.1.question: What is the main stylistic difference between Taurasi DOCG and Aglianico del Vulture DOC?
slides.8.questions.1.options.0: They are identical — different names for the same area
slides.8.questions.1.options.1: Taurasi is weightier with black fruit + tar; Aglianico del Vulture is more elegant with more pronounced volcanic minerality
slides.8.questions.1.options.2: Taurasi is a white-wine area, Vulture a red-wine area
slides.8.questions.1.explanation: Taurasi (Campania, clay-limestone) is weightier with black fruit + tar; Aglianico del Vulture (Basilicata, volcanic tuff) is more elegant, with a more pronounced smoky volcanic minerality — one of the most exciting terroir comparisons within a single grape.
slides.8.questions.2.question: What is the historical significance of Gaglioppo's Cirò DOC?
slides.8.questions.2.options.2: A wine of Greek colonial times with over 2,700 years of history, said to have been the victory wine of Olympic athletes
slides.8.questions.2.explanation: Cirò DOC is one of Italy's oldest wines: Greek colonists (Magna Graecia) planted Gaglioppo on the Calabrian coast over 2,700 years ago, and legend says it was the victory wine awarded to ancient Olympic athletes.
slides.8.questions.3.question: What is the relationship between Primitivo and Zinfandel?
slides.8.questions.3.options.1: Zinfandel is a descendant of Primitivo
slides.8.questions.3.options.2: They are the same variety; DNA research confirmed both come from Croatia's Tribidrag
slides.8.questions.3.options.3: Primitivo is an improved form of Zinfandel
slides.8.questions.3.explanation: UC Davis DNA comparison in 1994 proved that Primitivo (Puglia, Italy) and Zinfandel (California, US) are the same variety, and in 2001 it was traced to Croatia's Crljenak Kaštelanski (old name Tribidrag).
slides.8.questions.4.question: What is the main stylistic difference between Greco di Tufo and Fiano di Avellino?
slides.8.questions.4.options.0: Greco is a red grape, Fiano a white grape
slides.8.questions.4.options.1: Greco is strongly mineral with sulphurous flint; Fiano is round and creamy with honey and hazelnut
slides.8.questions.4.options.2: They are almost identical in style
slides.8.questions.4.explanation: Greco di Tufo DOCG gets minerality and a sulphurous flinty note from its tuff soils; Fiano di Avellino DOCG is known for its round, creamy texture, honey and hazelnut — Campania's two great whites complement each other perfectly.
slides.8.questions.5.question: What does the name Negroamaro mean, and what is its most famous wine style?
slides.8.questions.5.options.1: "Black bitter"; famous for Rosato (Leone de Castris's Five Roses)
slides.8.questions.5.explanation: The name Negroamaro is often explained as "Negro (black) + Amaro (bitter)"; Leone de Castris's Five Roses Rosato (1943, often called Italy's first bottled rosé sold commercially) is the grape's most famous wine.
slides.8.questions.6.question: What is the main reason for Etna DOC's fast-rising international reputation in recent years?
slides.8.questions.6.options.1: Pioneering producers, strong praise from international critics, plus the scarcity of old vines and contrada terroir
slides.8.questions.6.options.2: Eruptions of Etna raising its profile
slides.8.questions.6.options.3: Sicily becoming a tourist hotspot and driving wine sales
slides.8.questions.6.explanation: From the 2000s, pioneering producers such as Cornelissen, Terre Nere and Passopisciaro arrived and strong praise from international critics drew collectors' attention; together with the scarcity of Etna's old vines (60-100 years old) and the contrada terroir officially labelled since 2011, prices of top wines have risen markedly.
